# Jeremiah 39: Notes for a verse-by-verse commentary

**Before you use these notes:**
- **Sources:** Most of what I found comes from older commentaries collected on biblehub, studylight and blueletterbible, plus Guzik (enduringword), Constable and Utley (bible.org).
- **No real denominational split:** I didn't find Protestant traditions disagreeing on this chapter. The tradition-labelled views below (Calvin, Clarke, Coffman, Chuck Smith) largely agree. The closest thing to a debate is v. 18, on how faith and good deeds relate.
- **Not found:** I found nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca), netbible notes, bibleodyssey, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Those are left out. The only Catholic item is a brief Haydock note on studylight.
- **Copied text:** The enduringword, Pulpit Commentary and bible.org pages have no citation markers, so I've summarised them and linked them.

---

**Overview (vv. 1–18)**
- The chapter has two parts: the fall of Jerusalem with what happened to Zedekiah and to Jeremiah, then the promise of safety to Ebed-melech. (JFB) https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_039.cfm
- Constable sees the chapter as faithfulness set against faithlessness. Jeremiah and Ebed-melech stand for those who are faithful to God, and Zedekiah for faithlessness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-39.html
- Guzik lists ten things Jeremiah had foretold that came true here: disaster from the north, siege, famine, fire, exile and others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
- **Critical view:** The Pulpit Commentary calls the chapter "very confused" as it stands. It thinks vv. 1–2 and 4–13 were inserted later, noting that the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) leaves out vv. 4–13. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-39.html
- Remmers' book overview agrees that the Septuagint omits 39:4-13, among other passages. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik explains how a siege worked: the city was cut off and starved until it surrendered or its walls gave way. He links the suffering to Lamentations 4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
- Utley says the siege began in 589 BC and lasted nineteen months. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- **Dates differ between sources:**
  - Ellicott gives 590–588 BC (siege of eighteen months) and says famine ended it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/39.htm
  - Kidner (quoted by Guzik) gives 10 January 588 to 9 July 587. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: everything happened as Jeremiah said. Egypt did not rescue Judah, God did not step in as he had against Assyria, and the false prophets were shown to be wrong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
- Matthew Henry: Jerusalem's people thought it could never be taken, but sin provoked God to withdraw his protection, and then it was as weak as other cities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-3.htm

**v. 3**
- **Meaning of the scene:** Sitting in the gate showed the Babylonians now owned the city. Guzik compares it to an enemy taking over the Oval Office. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
- Gates were often places where legal matters were settled, so sitting there meant judging and governing (Bible Hub study notes). https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/39-3.htm
- Matthew Henry contrasts the people who used to sit there with these men. Godly officials whose names honoured Israel's God were replaced by men who bore the names of the heathen gods. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-3.html
- **How many officials?** Sources disagree on which words are names and which are titles.
  - Clarke cites Blayney, who thinks there are three, as the name that follows each is a title of office, not six people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-3.html
  - Utley lists the range: six in the Septuagint and KJV, five in Josephus, four in the RSV, three in the NIV, two in the NJB. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- **"Rabmag":** Ellicott (on the biblehub page) says this man appears in Assyrian records and played a prominent part afterwards as murdering Evil-merodach, the son of Nebuchadnezzar. He later ruled as Neriglissar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-3.htm
- **What "Rabmag" means is disputed:**
  - JFB takes it as "chief of the magi" (wise men), brought along to predict the outcome by astrology. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-3.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says linking "mag" to the Magi is a mistake. It suggests "high priest" or "chief of the sorcerers." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-39.html
  - The Restoration Commentary says both titles belonged to senior officials whose exact duties are unknown. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-39.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the king fled not only from Babylon but from God's promised judgment. Kidner adds that Zedekiah now abandoned the people he had doomed. Guzik also cites Ezekiel 12:12, which predicted this flight. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
- **Route:** Utley links the king's garden to the Pool of Siloam and says Josephus puts the escape at midnight. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- Keil & Delitzsch: even then, escape was still possible through the south gate, at the king's garden, between the two walls. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-7.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Zedekiah was caught close to the Jordan and possible safety. Maclaren says the hope of escape only made capture more bitter, and Morgan that "there is no escape from God." This fulfils Jeremiah 32:4 and 34:3 (he would meet Nebuchadnezzar face to face). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
- **"Pronounced judgment":** JFB says Zedekiah was tried as a common criminal, not as a king. He had violated his oath of loyalty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-39.html
- Utley: Riblah was Nebuchadnezzar's main field camp, about fifty miles north of Damascus. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39

**v. 6**
- Matthew Henry: Zedekiah was only thirty-two, so they must all be little, some of them infants. Zedekiah had been warned of this in 38:23. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_039.cfm
- Guzik: the nobles who had hated Jeremiah (38:4) were justly judged. Maclaren notes that these killings also guarded against any future revolt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/

**v. 7**
- **Two prophecies fulfilled:** Zedekiah saw the king of Babylon (Jer. 32:4), yet though he was to die in Babylon, he should never see it (Ezekiel 12:13) (Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/39-7.htm
- Gill on the same page treats this as proof of God's foreknowledge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-7.htm
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): He went to Babylon, but Nebuchadnezzar had put out his eyes so he never saw it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-7.html
- **Spiritual blindness:** Matthew Henry says he was condemned to darkness who had shut his eyes against the clear light of God's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-7.htm
- Guzik and Trapp make the same point: the eyes of his mind had been put out long before. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
- **Calvin (Reformed):** because Zedekiah had hardened himself for so long, it was therefore just that he should die by little and little, and not be killed at once. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-7.html
- **Bronze chains:** Ellicott says the Hebrew is literally "two" bronze chains. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/39-7.htm
- **What happened to him later:** Ellicott notes that when Jehoiachin was released 26 years later, Zedekiah isn't mentioned, so it is a natural inference that his sufferings had ended previously. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Utley: the Hebrew has "house" (singular) of the people. Some take it as a meeting hall, the Temple, or (following the Talmud) the main synagogue. Kimchi's reading "the people's houses" shaped the English versions. Burnt limestone walls could not be reused for building. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- Guzik: Scripture tells the fall of Jerusalem four times (here, Jer. 52, 2 Kings 25, 2 Chron. 36). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/

**v. 9**
- **The title "captain of the guard":** Utley says it literally means "chief slaughterer," and it is unclear whether it meant executioner or chief cook. Some versions (NJB, REB) find a third group of exiles, "artisans," by changing the Hebrew to match 52:15. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- JFB thinks those exiled included the bondmen whom their Jewish brethren had enslaved once and again in violation of God's command (Jeremiah 34:8-20). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-39.html
- Guzik: Maclaren says the victor might think the god Nebo had beaten the LORD, but the defeated knew the LORD had kept his word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/

**v. 10**
- **Practical reason:** Constable says it was in Babylon's best interests to maintain the agricultural productivity of Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-10.html
- **God's justice:** JFB says those who before had been stripped of their possessions by the wealthier Jews obtain, not only their own, but those of others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-10.htm
- Gill likewise sees the justice of God in the oppressed receiving the land of their oppressors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-10.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed)** sees two sides. Poverty is often an advantage. But he also thinks Nebuzaradan wanted to rouse the envy of the exiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-10.html
- **Clarke (Wesleyan/Methodist)** is blunter: these were the leftovers of the population, not worth taking away. Same page.
- **Pentecost (Biblical Illustrator)** applies it to the Beatitudes: the poor in spirit and the meek inheriting. Same page.
- **Haydock (Catholic):** the land grant attached them to the Chaldeans, binding them to their new rulers. Same page.

**vv. 11–12**
- **How Nebuchadnezzar knew of Jeremiah:**
  - JFB suggests word came through deserters and through the Jews exiled earlier with Jeconiah. Hence, the king's kindness to him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-39.html
  - Utley lists Daniel, deserters or spies. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- **Pulpit homily:** the Babylonians probably thought Jeremiah was on their side, though his motives were patriotic. It also says God can use "fierce despots" to carry out his grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-39.html
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah saw the more of the hand of God because his deliverance came through the king of Babylon. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_039.cfm

**v. 13**
- The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott suggest Nebushazban may be another form of the "Sarsechim" named in v. 3, who holds the same title. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/39.htm

**v. 14**
- **The puzzle:** this verse seems to clash with 40:1–5, where Jeremiah is freed in chains at Ramah.
  - Ellicott suggests he was at first sent back to the prison where he had been found, till he could be placed under the protection of Gedaliah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-14.html
  - Maurer (cited by JFB) treats them as two separate releases. Same page.
  - The Pulpit Commentary prefers the fuller account in chapter 40. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-39.html
  - Utley says scholars simply don't know whether these are two accounts of one event or two events in order. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- **Gedaliah:** his father Ahikam had protected Jeremiah before (26:24). Gedaliah later became governor and was not of David's line (Utley). https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- **Pulpit homily:** Jeremiah chose to stay "among the people," a pastor staying with his flock and an example of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-39.html

**v. 15**
- **Timing:** this message came earlier, soon after Ebed-melech's rescue of Jeremiah. It is placed here so as not to break up the story (Keil & Delitzsch; Barnes). Hence היה, Jeremiah 39:15, is to be translated as a pluperfect, meaning "had come." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-16.htm
- Matthew Henry: it is told now to show that both Jeremiah and Ebed-melech were spared. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_039.cfm

**v. 16**
- **"Go" while in prison?**
  - The Pulpit Commentary and Keil say Ebed-melech must have visited Jeremiah in the courtyard. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-16.htm
  - Calvin (Reformed) draws a lesson: not to bring down God's word to our judgment, when anything is promised beyond our expectation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-15.html
- **"The Cushite" (Ethiopian):** Matthew Poole says calling him this rebukes the Jews, since a foreigner was kinder to the prophet. He sees it as a type of the calling of the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-16.htm
- Maclaren links Ebed-melech to the Ethiopian eunuch Philip met (Acts 8). https://biblehub.com/study/jeremiah/39-7.htm
- Guzik notes he was a Gentile who was barred from the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
- **Pulpit homily (Muir):** speaking in the name of "the God of Israel" signals that Ebed-melech is now counted a true Israelite. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-39.html

**v. 17**
- **"The men whom you fear":**
  - Ellicott: the princes whom he had irritated by his interference on behalf of Jeremiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-16.htm
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement) thinks this fear explains why thirty men were used in the rescue. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-15.html
- Ellicott also notes the promise is worded like the one to Baruch in 45:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-16.htm

**v. 18**
- **"Your life as a spoil of war":** JFB says the life he had risked would be his reward. He would be spared beyond all hope, when the lives of his enemies should be forfeited. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_039.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the same phrase in 21:9 and 38:2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-39.html
- Utley: "surely rescue" is an emphatic Hebrew form (the verb doubled for force). https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-39
- **Faith and works:** this is the nearest thing to a real difference of emphasis, though all agree faith was the root.
  - The Pulpit homily says the kind act alone would not have been enough to have secured him a Divine promise. Faith must show itself in deeds, but trust is the sole and universal condition. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-39.html
  - Calvin (Reformed): his mercy was the fruit and evidence of faith, for unbelief is always timid. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-18.html
  - Matthew Henry speaks of reward. God recompenses men's services according to their principles, and it is a prophet's reward (Matthew 10:41). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/39-16.htm
  - Coffman (Restoration/Arminian) calls trust his "salvation," normative also for Christians (Acts 16:31). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/39-18.html
  - Kidner (in Guzik) notes the text praises only his faith, not his courage. Trapp says believers today hold the same promises by faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-39/
  - Ryken (in Guzik): Like all true servants of the King, Ebed-Melech was saved by faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-38/
